items.question: Why did the professor say socioemotional selectivity is not about low energy or simple withdrawal?
items.notes: Likely when a student says older adults narrow relationships because they get tired or lose social interest.

items.question: How can socioemotional selectivity apply to students as well as older adults?
items.notes: The professor explicitly used the limited-time perception frame beyond old age.

items.question: Why is the SOC model important in gerontology rather than just a generic coping slogan?
items.notes: Likely when a student can name selection, optimization, compensation but cannot explain why the model matters for aging.

items.question: What is the better question: does experience change personality, or does personality channel people into certain experiences?
items.notes: This is one of the clearest professor-style distinction questions in the session.

items.question: What does it mean to say personality is stable if some traits still show age-related change?
items.notes: Likely when a student collapses rank-order stability and mean-level change into one vague claim.

items.question: Why did the professor use the Type A chair story, and what is the real mechanism claim behind it?
items.notes: Likely when a student remembers the anecdote but not the long-term behavioral pathway from trait to health outcome.

items.question: What is the difference between Erikson, Loevinger, and Levinson in this chapter, and which one gets the strongest criticism in lecture?
items.notes: The professor repeatedly distinguishes useful insight from weak empirical grounding.

items.question: Why is older adulthood not described here as automatic decline in emotion or happiness?
items.notes: Likely when a student speaks as if aging simply means more fear, sadness, and social loss.
